name: Nickel
lede: Nickel is a neutral mid grey named for the metal; the books say little about the grey itself, but a good deal about nickel's greens, yellows and one famous black.

sections.title: Which nickel
sections.body:
The swatch is a neutral mid grey, ISCC-NBS block 22 of 1955, named "medium gray" at a distance of 7.7 units, and Munsell N 4.8 [13]. Nothing in the books treats nickel as a color word the way they treat [[cobalt]] or [[copper]]. The name appears in the 1955 color circular and has no earlier record in our sources [13].

A flat grey square cannot carry what makes a metal look like a metal, which is its sheen. So the page is best read as the grey of a worn, satin nickel surface, and the rest of this article is about what the books say on nickel as a chemical ingredient of other colors [13]. They say more than the swatch suggests, and almost all of it is about green, yellow and black.

sections.title: The color of a metal's salts
sections.body:
Ball opens his chapter on pigments from the elements with a rough map. Iron claims red, copper the turquoise of its salts and the green of weathered copperwork, cobalt a deep blue, and nickel a sea-green, while chromium hesitates [1]. He is careful to add that these are not rigid identities, since copper can also make rust-red salts and iron can make greens and yellows [1].

Nickel's green is easy to see in a mineral. Annabergite, a nickel arsenate, is a green mineral known as nickel bloom and sometimes called nickel ochre [2]. Its cousin is cobalt's more famous bloom, described below [3][4].

sections.title: Cobalt's difficult neighbor
sections.body:
Cobalt's chief ore, smaltite, is also a nickel ore: it combines the arsenides of both metals and is found in silver mines [3][4]. Exposed to air it forms a brilliant blue fibrous crystal that miners called cobalt bloom [3][4]. It is a dangerous flower, because the arsenic in the mineral dust is toxic and corrosive [3].

The name cobalt itself comes from German *kobold*, a mischievous sprite that miners blamed for the poisonous nature of the mines [4]. Ball notes that cobalt ore is abundant in Saxony, where Georgius Agricola's *De re metallica* of 1556 warned silver miners about it [3]. The books do not explain how nickel got its own name.

sections.title: Nickel in modern pigments
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium says that nickel occurs primarily in synthetic pigments of recent origin [5]. One is nickel rutile yellow, with the approximate composition titanium, antimony and nickel oxide, listed in the Colour Index as Pigment Yellow 53 and described as a light lemon yellow [5]. It also goes by the trade names sun yellow and titan yellow [5]. A related barium-nickel-titanium yellow, called priderite yellow after a mineral of the same crystal structure, is used chiefly in ceramics, though it is sold as a paint pigment too [6]. Gurney's table of artists' pigments lists both nickel dioxine yellow and nickel titanate yellow among the yellows that painters can buy [7].

Nickel also modifies other colors. Replacing magnesium with nickel in a cobalt-zinc titanate spinel gives a brilliant cobalt green, and a lithium-based formula that also contains nickel gives a turquoise [8]. In metal-complex azo pigments, the dye is usually chelated with nickel, less often with cobalt or iron [9]. In 1946 Du Pont described a nickel azo complex that it marketed as Green Gold, listed as Pigment Green 10, and a second nickel azo complex became Pigment Yellow 150 [9][10].

There were earlier attempts. Salter in 1869 noted that nickel yields a pleasing yellowish brown, clear in thin washes and fuller in oil [11]. Early twentieth-century sources describe a nickel yellow made by precipitating nickel sulphate with sodium phosphate: the precipitate is pale green and turns bright yellow at a red heat [11].

sections.title: The nickel black
sections.body: Paterson calls NPL Super Black the darkest colour ever developed [12]. It is a coating of nickel alloy and phosphorus from the National Physical Laboratory, said to be 25 times darker than common black paint, and it takes in 97.7 per cent of light shone from above [12]. A grey metal, treated, becomes the opposite of itself.

sections.title: Nickel, iron and the sky
sections.body: Nickel appears in a gem story as well. The meteorite type called pallasite, first described by Peter Simon Pallas in 1772, is made of peridot crystals set in what was once a paste of nickel and iron [14]. Finlay likens a cross-section to a piece of modern jewellery: green crystals glinting in a silvery metal lattice [14]. Here the grey of nickel and the green of its minerals sit side by side.

sections.title: A healing theory
sections.body:
The color-healing writer Edwin Babbitt claimed that coloured light carried the elements of the substances that matched it [15]. In his scheme, blue light carried sulphur, copper, nickel, cobalt, cadmium and manganese [15]. This is the chromotherapy tradition, and the claim that colors heal is a myth: Birren records that Babbitt's followers were bitterly attacked by medical bodies [15].

Aldous Huxley, in a passage that Batchelor quotes, complained of a modern glut of glass, chrome and nickel, whose bathroom and kitchen reflections had dulled the old thrill of shining surfaces [16]. For Huxley, then, chrome and nickel were the shine of the everyday modern home [16].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units (ΔE2000) of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,171 of them, or 4.9 per cent [13]. The rate is flat through the early centuries, about 3.6 per cent in the 1400s and 1500s, and then peaks sharply in the 1930s, in 11 of 69 paintings, or 16 per cent [13].

The painter who returns to it most often, among those with enough works, is [[painter:claude-monet|Monet]], with 15 of 50, followed by Shen Zhou with 6 of 12 and Frederic Remington with 6 of 16 [13]. Impressionism as a movement carries it in 24 of 140 works, 3.5 times the archive rate [13]. Among single canvases it covers the most of Whistler's [[painting:aic-14309|Coast Scene, Bathers]], at 72 per cent, Homer's [[painting:cma-106088|Early Morning After a Storm at Sea]], at 60 per cent, and Manet's [[painting:commons-Q17494570|Flowers in a Crystal Vase]], at 59 per cent [13].

Inside a painting it usually plays a mid-tone (53 per cent), and a third of the time a light (34 per cent) [13]. It keeps company with [[slate-grey]], [[grey]], [[charcoal-grey]] and [[silver]] [13]. In printed English the adjective *nickel* peaks in the 1960s and rose fastest in the 1930s [13]. As photographed, these are varnished paintings, and a grey match is the easiest of all to get from a dulled varnish, so none of this is a pigment test [13].
